title: Cas3-mediated genome reduction: demonstration in Cupriavidus necator H16 improves growth on heterotrophic and autotrophic carbon sources.
data_url: https://github.com/akirakaren/map_Tninsertions/tree/main/Fulk2026_result_summary (processed transposon insertion tables); NCBI SRA BioProject PRJNA1433156 (raw reads only)

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and opened insertion_sites.xlsx (1.25 MB) from the authors' GitHub repo: 6 sheets, 4,357 insertion rows for library lib023 and 5,054 for lib123 (14 columns each: replicon, coordinate, strand, raw and deduplicated read counts, gene_id/locus_tag, position within gene), per-gene sheets with 2,587 and 2,841 genes, and a combined sheet with 3,905 genes. Read the repo README (pipeline, reference GCF_000009285.1) and the summary stats file (31,112 deduplicated reads at sites, 98.5% duplication, median 1 read per site, 3,902 intragenic vs 455 intergenic sites, 2,587 of 6,710 annotated genes hit = 38.6%). Queried NCBI for BioProject PRJNA1433156: 21 runs, raw sequence reads only (first run 91,009 long reads, 372 MB).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything about the mutant phenotypes: the 16 unique large deletions and their 2-5 bp microhomologies, the per-isolate growth rates (25% faster on fructose, 14% faster on formate), the background single-nucleotide and small-indel mutations in waaC, phcR, ptsP, E6A55_03500 and E6A55_01580. These live in Supplementary Tables S1-S3, which I could not retrieve: the Europe PMC supplementary-files endpoint returned HTTP 500 and the publisher site is off-limits by project policy.

a1_downloadable.note: One processed table (insertion_sites.xlsx, 1.25 MB) downloads with no login from the authors' GitHub. But the paper's own Data Availability names only raw reads in SRA (PRJNA1433156), which project policy excludes, and the phenotype tables (Supplementary S1-S3) were not retrievable.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: No column anywhere says 'this region is dispensable' or gives a fitness effect of a deletion. That label would have to be built by joining deletion coordinates in a supplementary table to growth rates shown in figures, for a handful of isolates that also carry unrelated background mutations.

a3_inputs_present.note: Genome coordinates and locus tags are in the table and the reference genome (GCF_000009285.1) is a single free download, so gene and protein sequences are obtainable without thousands of lookups.

a4_units_stated.note: Checked in the file: columns are raw and deduplicated read counts, unique sites per kilobase, and relative position in gene, all defined in the repo README.

a5_enough_rows.note: The paper reports 16 unique large deletions across roughly 25 sequenced isolates; growth rates were measured for 3-5 isolates per condition. That is far under the ~400 rows needed even for classification. Read from the paper text, since the supplementary tables would not download.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Opened it in pandas in seconds; the reference genome adds about 7 MB.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The file reproduces the paper's stated counts exactly: 4,357 unique insertions for the CHC023 library and 5,054 for the CHC123 library.

a8_label_provenance.note: For the only large-n alternative (per-gene transposon insertion count as a proxy for gene essentiality) the label is driven by gene length and Tn5 sequence preference, i.e. by the features themselves, and the library is far from saturating: 9,411 sites over a 7.4 Mb genome, median 1 read per site, only 38.6% of genes hit, so 'no insertion' is mostly sampling noise, not biology. Verified these numbers in the files.

existing_models.name: DeeplyEssential (2020), a neural network predicting bacterial essential genes from gene and protein sequence features
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported to outperform earlier classifiers on 30 bacterial species from the DEG (Database of Essential Genes); split details from the abstract only, I did not retrieve the full paper.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved; the abstract emphasises avoiding structural or network features that are often unavailable.

existing_models.name: CNN4Essential (2026), a convolutional network for bacterial gene essentiality using fused features
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved beyond the search listing, so no number recorded.

existing_models.name: DELEAT (2021), a tool that classifies gene essentiality and designs large genome deletions
existing_models.score_and_split: Logistic regression on six sequence-derived gene features, no experimental data needed; score not retrieved.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (a protein language model) or Nucleotide Transformer (a DNA language model)
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU would suffice for 6,710 genes
backbone.licence: ESM-2 is MIT-licensed; not reached, because the label fails first.

integration.partner_dataset: DEG (Database of Essential Genes) and the published RB-TnSeq fitness study in C. necator cited by this paper
integration.join_key: locus tag / gene identifier (H16_RS* or E6A55_*), with an identifier mapping needed between the two annotation schemes
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does sequence-predicted gene essentiality from other bacteria transfer to which regions of C. necator can actually be deleted? Worth asking, but this paper supplies only 16 deletions to test it on.

controls.positive_control: A working pipeline must show near-zero insertions in textbook essential genes such as dnaA, gyrB and ribosomal protein genes; in the file dnaA and gyrB do carry insertions, which itself shows the library is not saturating enough to call essentiality.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle per-gene insertion counts across genes and confirm any signal collapses; also train on gene length alone, which likely explains most of the count.
controls.external_validation: The earlier transposon-mutagenesis fitness study in C. necator referenced in the discussion, and DEG essentiality calls in related bacteria.

honest_claim_h3: Any model built from what is downloadable here could claim only 'predicts how many transposon insertions a gene received in two shallow, non-saturating libraries from one lab', not 'predicts whether deleting a region improves growth' — the growth phenotype exists for roughly 16 deletions in a single strain background.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use genome sequence to predict which chunks of a bacterium's genome can be deleted to make it grow faster.
plain_idea.train_on: The project considered would train on genomic regions of Cupriavidus necator H16, a bacterium used industrially to turn carbon dioxide or formate into products, described by sequence and gene content. Verified counts available: 9,411 transposon insertion sites and 6,710 annotated genes, but only 16 unique measured deletions.
plain_idea.predict: Whether removing a region speeds up growth, ideally as the measured maximum growth rate from shake-flask and bioreactor cultures. Those growth rates were measured for only a few isolates per condition, and the values sit in figures and in supplementary tables I could not download.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Strain-engineering groups building carbon-dioxide-fixing production hosts currently find deletable regions by trial and error; a predictor would save months of library building. As it stands, this paper has the tool but not enough labelled outcomes to train one.

more_or_better_data.why: Existing essentiality predictors train on DEG across about 30 bacterial species; this paper adds two shallow insertion libraries from one strain (31,112 deduplicated reads total) and 16 measured deletions.

confidence_score.why: There are two libraries, but they are the same protocol in the same lab on related strains, and median depth is 1 read per site, so they cannot support calibrated per-gene uncertainty.

models_beatable.why: DeeplyEssential (2020) and DELEAT (2021, logistic regression) are old and simple enough to beat with a protein language model, but beating them needs a trustworthy essentiality label, which this dataset does not provide.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails the first condition: the quantity measured here (transposon insertion counts in a non-saturating library) is not the same quantity those models predict (curated essentiality), so adding it does not improve them by construction.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: predict which genomic regions of Cupriavidus necator H16 can be deleted for a growth benefit, from sequence features, using this paper's Cas3-generated deletions as labels. The measured outcome exists for only 16 unique deletions in roughly 25 isolates, and the one large table that does download (9,411 mapped transposon insertion sites, 6,710 genes) measures sequencing coverage of a shallow library rather than any biological fitness, with insertion counts driven by gene length.

effort.compute_note: Timed the actual spreadsheet load (seconds, under 1 GB RAM); embedding hours is an estimate for ESM-2 small on 6,710 proteins at roughly 0.5 proteins/second on a laptop CPU, not measured.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count how many deletions have a measured growth rate. The paper's own text answers it: 16 unique deletions, 3-5 phenotyped isolates per condition. That kills it in five minutes.

verdict_reason: A5 fails outright: the phenotype of interest (growth benefit of a deletion) exists for 16 unique deletions in about 25 isolates, two orders of magnitude short of the minimum. A2 also fails, because no column records a deletion's fitness effect; it would have to be inferred by joining supplementary tables to figure panels, with confounding background mutations in each isolate. The only large downloadable table (verified: 4,357 + 5,054 mapped transposon insertion sites, 3,905 genes with any insertion out of 6,710) fails A8 as a stand-in label: with 31,112 deduplicated reads, median 1 read per site and insertions even in essential genes such as dnaA and gyrB, insertion count reflects library shallowness and gene length rather than essentiality, and open models (DeeplyEssential, DELEAT) already cover that task with better labels from the Database of Essential Genes. Good paper, excellent data hygiene by the authors, wrong shape for machine learning.
